Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years.
Intel, Microsoft and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from its leadership crisis.
As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel.
“Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch.
Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen.
The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.”
Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list .
Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away.
According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.”
Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips .
Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.”
And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s.
“These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said.

Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but there were no further details over how many prisoners would be exchanged or when it would happen.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it was to have European delegates "at the table".
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told the BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of European leaders gathered in Dublin on Thursday that he believed the security of the region had been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
Starshield technology, which was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use, has played a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

Unlike a bulky and almost always noisy treadmill , the best walking pad is a slim (ideally portable) machine that can slide under your standing desk or fit anywhere in your home. I’m also convinced that walking pads make me more productive. Not only do you crush your daily steps before 5 pm, but daily use can boost your energy levels, mood, and cardiovascular health. Walking on an incline also strengthens and tones your lower-body muscles, so you can even get a decent workout in. There are tons on the market, offering varying speed capabilities, extra features like built-in desk platforms and wheels, and durability. Our remote testers clocked serious hours walking, working, and sometimes jogging to find the best walking pads worth the space and money.

Size and storage: Walking pads are typically much smaller than traditional treadmills, but check the product dimensions and make sure the footprint will work for you. If you’re working with an especially small space, consider a foldable or under-desk walking pad. If you’re planning to store it under furniture or in a closet when not in use, shop for slimmer models with wheels for portability.
Belt size and track length: The deck size is dependent on the product’s dimensions, and you should take into consideration how much space you have to work with. But, generally, I prefer wider and lengthier belts that feel more stable to walk on, especially if you’re on the taller side or have a longer stride.
Weight capacity: Walking pads aren’t as durable as treadmills and tend to have a lower weight capacity. Check the machine’s limit, and make sure it will work for you and anyone else in the household who will be using it. Per the online reviews we’ve read, walking pads are notorious for falling apart after only a few years or even a few months of use, so it might be worth getting something that’s a little more heavy-duty.
Speed range: Choose a walking pad that offers a speed range that best fits your lifestyle and goals. Most models will generally offer speeds up to 4 mph, which should cover everything from gentle strolls and brisk walks, and is ideal for home office use. There are walking pad-treadmill hybrids that offer faster paces if you’re also looking for a jog.
Adjustable inclines: Some models remain flat, but I prefer the walking pads that feature adjustable levels so that you can customize your cardio intensity as you see fit. Walking at an incline can also strengthen your lower body muscles and reduce anterior knee loading.
Metrics and display: Most walking pads have an LED display that tracks your steps, distance, time, and calories. Some models also include a remote control and/or app, which can sometimes sync your metrics from the machine, so you can check your workout data on your phone. This may not matter to you if you prefer to use your Apple Watch or fitness tracker .
Price: You can snag a solid, no-frills walking pad for under $300, but if you’re looking for a higher-end model with a surplus of features, it can cost $500+.

Finland says Ukraine struck a Russian warship near its coast as Kyiv and Moscow held US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.
Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region.
The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February.
It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea .
So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know:
“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement.
The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected.
It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg.
On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain.
Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia.
Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv.
“We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle.
But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe.
Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic.
“Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks.
“According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts.
Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year.
The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks.
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO.
Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday.
The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported.
On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland.
“Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries, ports, and energy infrastructure to raise the economic cost of Moscow’s war effort.

Russia has not commented publicly on the reported strike on its warship.
Governor Drozdenko said 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region during Wednesday’s attack, which also cut off a power station.

Patrick Makau, a member of Kenya’s parliament representing Mavoko, the constituency that includes Syokimau, urged rescue agencies in a post on social media to act quickly.

The nuclear agency has not been able to inspect any sites attacked by the US and Israel last year
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.
Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.
"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.
The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.
The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

Tehran has told the IAEA that it is not possible to resume inspections in the current security situation.
The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme.
Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation.
The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported.
The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”.
The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.
Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility.
Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it.
The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities.

Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.

Exclusive: Sources reveal party is covering costs – raising new questions about leader’s explanation for billionaire’s gift
Nigel Farage’s personal security has been paid for out of Reform UK’s central funds despite his claim that these expenses would be covered by an undisclosed gift of £5m from a billionaire donor, sources have told the Guardian.
The Reform leader has had the central party pay for a team and two cars ever since a reduction in the security provided by the taxpayer after a review in 2025.
The disclosure raises fresh questions about Farage’s explanation of the £5m he was given by the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
After the Guardian revealed the gift , Harborne said it was intended “to support Nigel’s security not just now but for the rest of his life”.
Farage initially said: “This money was given to me so that I would be safe and secure for the rest of my life.”
He suggested that the Home Office did not offer him any security support. In fact, though it was reduced in scale, he was offered a bodyguard, a driver and car – similar to the provision made for Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the official opposition.
Farage refused this, and since then his security has been paid for from central party funds. These costs have amounted to more than £150,000 in the past year, sources said.
The arrangement has caused consternation for some within the party. “It’s completely at odds with the narrative he’s tried to sell the public,” a Reform source said.
Asked about Farage expensing the party, a spokesperson for Reform UK said: “As a standard practice, we do not comment on security matters.”
The party refused to answer questions about whether Farage had spent any of the £5m on security costs to date. It also refused to address questions about why Farage had refused the offer of a taxpayer-funded package.
The Guardian understands that the party makes a distinction between security required as a result of its leader’s political activities, which it pays for, and his potential longer-term personal security needs, which the gift was intended to provide for.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses over his secret £5m ‘gift’ have fallen apart. You can’t trust a word he says. From secret gifts, to police investigations into Reform’s finances, to donations from a convicted fraudster – Reform are up to their necks in sleaze and scandal. Farage and his party are simply not fit for office. It’s time for him to get his story straight and be honest with the public.”
A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Nigel Farage variously described his fishy bung from an overseas crypto billionaire as a reward for Brexit, cash he can spend on Ferraris or the horses if he wants, the list goes on. It is no wonder people are asking questions, and the public are entitled to a straight answer. Nigel Farage should come clean about where the £5m has gone and what it was really for.”
Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson for home affairs, complained publicly that the party was having to seek fresh support from donors to meet Farage’s security costs in October 2025.
Harborne gave Farage £5m shortly before he stood as an MP in the 2024 general election. On becoming an MP, Farage was offered and accepted taxpayer-funded security, which he used until the autumn of 2025.
Harborne had been the dominant party donor in recent years until he was joined by his fellow crypto tycoon Ben Delo in donating a further £36m each in September.
Costs charged to Reform by Farage have included security changes to his properties, including ones used by his family members, according to sources.
The security team funded by Reform has also been used by Farage for personal activities, sources said.
Since Harborne’s initial claim that the gift was intended to fund his security arrangements, Farage’s account of what the £5m gift was for has varied. He has said he could spend it on Ferraris, or that it was a reward for Brexit campaigning, and at other times he has tried to suggest it was not political but for his security for life.
Footage gathered by the undercover reporting group Verbatim and shared with the Guardian last month appeared to show that Farage’s close aide Dan Jukes believed it was a PR mistake for Farage to suggest it was for anything other than security.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said, after Farage suggested the money was a reward for his political campaigning in an interview with the Sun.
Jukes has since stood down from Reform and he denies any wrongdoing.
Lawyers for Harborne have previously said he “expected nothing in return” for the money and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.
The timeline for the gift is disputed. Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024. According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May , just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.
The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in 2024.

Bu sayede büyük kod tabanları ve uzun videolar gibi yoğun veri gerektiren yapay zeka uygulamalarının daha verimli çalışması hedefleniyor. Google'ın TPU müşterileri arasında Anthropic ve Apple gibi şirketler de bulunuyor. Şirketin yaklaşık 100 müşteriye ulaşması, yapay zeka donanımı pazarında Nvidia'ya alternatif çözümlere yönelik talebin arttığını gösteriyor.

Senior police officers are accused of illegally monitoring President Prabowo Subianto, exposing rival networks within Indonesia's security establishment and renewing concerns about political misuse of surveillance.
For decades, Indonesia's police and intelligence agencies have been accused of spying on politicians, journalists, and activists, Now, a widening scandal involving some of the country's most senior police officers has brought those concerns to the heart of government.
Earlier this month, Indonesian police named four senior officers as suspects in an alleged illegal surveillance operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures.
Former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was among the senior officers arrested. The ex-police chief became the president's chief of staff in October, just weeks before the scandal broke.
Investigators claim that officers intercepted communications without proper authorization in 2025 and 2026 and then tried to delete records of the operation.
Suyudi Ario Seto, the new police chief, told a parliamentary panel this week that the surveillance targeted the president, officials within the presidential palace, ministries, state institutions, lawmakers, political party figures, governors, anti-corruption officials, activists and students.
A parliamentary commission is investigating the motive behind the wiretapping operation and trying to uncover whether other senior figures were involved. Meanwhile, the police have opened an investigation into possible treason-related offenses.
Amnesty International has called for investigations to also determine whether the wiretap operation was used to intimidate government critics and weaken civil liberties.
The government has responded by ordering an additional 20,000 troops to Jakarta as a precaution, although there had been no indication that the wiretap is part of a larger campaign intended to bring down Prabowo's administration.
The affair has intensified tensions between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo, commonly known as Jokowi, while exposing deeper problems with the powers and political loyalties of Indonesia's security establishment.
"The use of surveillance is actually pretty widespread," Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor at Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani, told DW.
"While there are laws and regulations, they are flouted since there is no regulation on eavesdropping, especially by law enforcement agencies," he added.
Officially, Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions Law prohibits unauthorized interception, while other legislation permits surveillance for specified law enforcement and intelligence purposes.
Despite these safeguards against illegal interception, Sulaiman said it could be argued, "that the police and intelligence are essentially unconstrained."
Indonesia's intelligence agencies and law enforcement have long played a role in political competition, Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Under Suharto's authoritarian New Order regime, which collapsed in 1998, intelligence agencies were central in monitoring political opponents and suppressing dissent.
After democratization, controversies persisted . In 1999, a leaked recording of a telephone conversation involving then-President BJ Habibie raised concerns about surveillance within the presidential palace itself.
In 2024, the elite counterterrorism unit, Densus 88, was caught surveilling Deputy Attorney General Febrie Adriansyah, who at the time was overseeing major corruption investigations.
But what makes the latest allegations particularly significant is "their apparent scale and the suggestion that surveillance capabilities may have been deployed outside established legal procedures and against the sitting president," Priyandita said.
Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo, a former special forces general, has sought to consolidate his authority over the country's political and security institutions.
Critics accuse him of accelerating the militarization of civilian government, including through legislation expanding the military's ability to occupy civilian posts.
However, the president inherited a security establishment partly shaped by his predecessor.
In 2024, Jokowi, who couldn't run for office again, backed Prabowo's presidential campaign and his eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, became Prabowo's running mate and subsequently vice president.
The Jokowi-Prabowo alliance was decisive for Prabowo's electoral victory, but it also left him governing alongside officials and political networks cultivated during Jokowi's decade in power.
On Thursday, Jokowi's son Gibran resigned as vice president amid a growing controversy over his educational credentials.
Indonesia's Constitutional Court and the country's Supreme Court found that Gibran's overseas high school qualifications fell short of legal requirements for vice presidential candidates, and had been wrongly accepted by election authorities.
The academic credentials probe was apparently not related to the investigations into the wiretapping scandal.
A series of government reshuffles in recent months has also been interpreted as Prabowo's attempt to strengthen his control, especially against some Jokowi loyalists. Listyo, appointed police chief by Jokowi in 2021 and long regarded as close to the former president, was replaced in October.
"Prabowo may have consolidated his political authority since taking office, but that does not necessarily translate into complete control over institutions whose senior leadership and internal networks were shaped under the previous Jokowi government," Priyandita said.
Also, Prabowo may emerge politically stronger if the investigation weakens rival networks within the police. However, replacing one set of political loyalties with another would do little to resolve the underlying problem in the country's security apparatus.
The controversy has renewed calls for reforms that would prevent police surveillance capabilities from becoming instruments of political competition.
Because the latest wiretapping controversy targeted not only the president but also political elites and key civil society actors, "surveillance goes beyond mere politics," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, told DW.
"It is a calculated and systematic abuse of power," he added.
Fahrizal argued that a fundamental problem lies in the National Police's constitutional and institutional position, which answers directly to the president.
This increases the risk that the police respond to presidential political interests rather than solely to the law.
In November last year, Prabowo established a police reform commission to investigate longstanding concerns about professionalism, governance, and accountability.
However, Fahrizal said former police chief Listyo failed to implement meaningful reforms, with the latest allegations showing the consequences of inadequate oversight.
Fahrizal called for Indonesia to bring its fragmented surveillance regulations together under a unified legal framework, with tighter controls over the interception powers of the police's Criminal Investigation Agency and the Intelligence and Security Agency.
"Internal police reform must urgently address this by restoring professionalism and a proper institutional ethos," Fahrizal said.
Without such changes, divided political loyalties risk becoming a "dangerous virus" spreading through the police and other security institutions, he added.
